Falkirk 2-1 St Johnstone: Bairns hold on to beat Saints to extend Scottish Premiership winning run to six
Report as Falkirk beat St Johnstone 2-1; Jacob Murrell opened the scoring with Finley Barbrook doubling their lead; Josh Campbell pulled a goal back for Saints; Falkirk remain third in the Scottish Premiership; St Johnstone are seventh
Saturday 21 November 2026 17:46, UK
Falkirk clung on to clock up six top-flight wins in a row for the first time since 1966 with a 2-1 home victory over St Johnstone.
John McGlynn's team scored early in each half to remain third in the Scottish Premiership.
Jacob Murrell's eighth goal of a superb debut season sent the Bairns on their way inside six minutes and Finley Barbrook's second goal in as many games on 48 minutes doubled the advantage.
- Teams | Stats
- Watch FREE Scottish Prem highlights | Latest Scottish Prem news | Latest scores
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream the Scottish Prem with no contract
Josh Campbell nodded in a late reply to serve up a scare but the hosts held firm thereafter.
McGlynn's well-oiled machine continued to operate at a high level and their surprise bid for a European place shows no sign of stopping.
They went in front when a long Deniss Melniks throw-in was flicked on by stand-in skipper Liam Henderson and Murrell netted on the volley from close range.
Saints created a flurry of chances in response. The pick of them saw Campbell sent clear by Joel Cotterill. The on-loan Hibs forward opted for an early shot and skewed the effort a yard wide.
Top-scorer Josh Fowler found plenty of penalty-box space, too, but his strike was deflected wide.
Falkirk were next to threaten as play swept from end to end.
Toby Steward fumbled a Murrell header from Scott Tanser's delivery but recovered to deny Ethan Ross on his goal line.
Dan Finlayson bravely got his head in the way of a rocket shot from Owen Eames.
Falkirk 'keeper Scott Bain batted away from Taylor Steven and Fowler dragged a great chance wide - both set up by Kai Fotheringham.
Crucially for Falkirk, they were more clinical so close to goal.
Their second, three minutes into the second half, was sparked by Ross feeding Eames out wide. The Derby loan winger's rapid burst of pace did for Liam Smith. Eames fired across goal to award Barbrook with a tap-in from a yard out.
The game should have been over as a contest on 55 minutes but Ross miscued right in front of goal from Murrell's cross.
Simo Valakari made a trio of attack-minded changes, including Danny Schmidt for Fowler.
Within a minute, the German spurned a glorious chance. Campbell's pass was a touch behind the unmarked Schmidt and a weak shot was saved by the legs of Bain.
Falkirk managed the game well until conceding on 83 minutes.
Campbell gave Saints hope by ghosting onto substitute Logan Chalmers' delivery from deep and heading past Bain.
Saints 'keeper Steward joined the attack in the final seconds as a free-kick was launched into the box to no avail.
What the managers said...
Falkirk boss John McGlynn:
"I wouldn't have believed it if someone had said we would win six in a row this season.
"We only managed two in a row last season and thought we were doing well.
"To do six is beyond our wildest dreams, really.
"Since coming here, we have always tried to create history and break records.
"That has been unbeaten runs, the 'Invincible' season in League One and games against other teams.
"Winning at Easter Road for the first time in 20 years, beating Celtic for the first time in 19.
"Not many teams have won at Tynecastle recently and we were the first to win there in 18 months.
"We thrive on that. We are always the underdog and we are trying to prove people wrong."
St Johnstone manager Simo Valakari:
"We didn't give ourselves a chance today. For virtually the whole match we were chasing the game after conceding a goal early in the first half.
"We gifted them a platform and momentum. Then, after conceding a goal early in the second half, it was almost impossible to get back into the match.
"Our players didn't think it was impossible, though. They thought they could do it. But to go 2-0 down away from home against a top team is very hard.
"We are a strong team but we faced a team today that took its chances. We didn't, so we cannot complain."

items.text:
FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
- Published
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment.
When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.
"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," the president added.
This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

items.summary:

items.text:
Two changes for Newcastle from their draw with Fulham before the international break. Lewis Miley and Arsenal alumnus Joe Willock replaces Nico Gonzalez and Yoane Wissa.
Arsenal, who beat Hull 1-0 a fortnight ago, bring in Eberechi Eze for Christos Tzolis. That means Bruno Guimaraes will start against his old club. A frighteningly strong bench includes the great William Saliba, who has yet to play this season because of a back injury.
Mikel Arteta has said Bukayo Saka may not return before Christmas as the Arsenal forward continues his rehabilitation from a thigh injury.
Saka has been out since limping off against Bayern Munich at the end of last month, and it is understood he has yet to resume light training. Arteta revealed more tests during the international break confirmed the England forward did not need surgery and that he was expected to be out for another four weeks.
When asked whether Saka could be fit for the game against Manchester United on 20 December, Arteta was unsure. “I cannot be that specific,” he said. “In four weeks’ time a lot of things can happen. Maybe it is three and then it is five.
“At the end, there are a few elements. One is the healing of that tissue – and we cannot predict exactly when that tissue is going to be in the best condition to push it. Then there is the rehab plan that we have now, what he needs to do in the gym, what he needs to do in terms of treatment and on the field.”
With the temperature in Newcastle forecast to dip to 0C at kick-off, Matthias Jaissle is perhaps hoping that his team’s guests from north London (where a balmy 9C is predicted at 5.30pm) freeze in the Tyneside chill. Otherwise it is hard to envisage his young side overcoming a formidable looking Arsenal on a day when Newcastle’s head coach seeks what would be only his second win in seven games.
Home fans will not merely be hurt by the sight of their much-missed former captain Bruno Guimarães wearing Arsenal colours but decidedly nervous about a fixture that precedes a run of tricky engagements involving a trip to Brighton and home dates with Manchester United and Sunderland.
Jaissle’s cause could be helped should Mikel Arteta name Guimarães in his starting XI and the crowd respond to the once adored Brazilian’s defection by creating the sort of hostile atmosphere that might just galvanise a Newcastle team expected to contain the former Arsenal midfielder Joe Willock.
Meanwhile Jaissle’s defence must be mindful of the threat posed by another Newcastle old boy in Mikel Merino.
Arsenal have a unique relationship with the north of England. They’ve won titles at Anfield and Old Trafford, lost them at the Reebok Stadium, and there have been periods in history when every Arsenal trip beyond Watford Gap felt like a referendum on whether they had the necessary minerals.
Mikel Arteta’s side aren’t much different. For years, St James’ Park was a symbol of their inability to take the final step to glory. That changed last September, when Gabriel’s 96th-minute winner set up a different neural pathway that ultimately led to Arsenal becoming champions for the first time since 2004.
Newcastle (A) was a more intimidating prospect 14 months ago than it is today. St James’ Park hasn’t been much of a fortress this season, with Newcastle taking only five points from five home games under Matthias Jaissle. But just as Arsenal changed the narrative last season, so Newcastle can do the same today.

items.text:
India’s opposition stages protests against Meta over account removals
Youth wing of Congress party issues a seven-day ‘ultimatum’ to the US technology giant, urging it to lift all restrictions.
The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party has staged protests outside Meta offices in three cities, demanding that the United States technology company restore the Instagram accounts of its leaders.
The protests took place in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram, near New Delhi, on Friday and led to clashes with police and security guards, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress on Saturday.
In Hyderabad, protesters entered the building that houses Meta’s offices and clashed with police. In Mumbai, protesters spray-painted slogans on the walls outside, and in Gurugram they held banners reading “restore Youth Congress accounts”.
The party has alleged that on November 19, Meta illegally withheld the Instagram accounts of the youth wing’s president and the party official overseeing the wing on orders from the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
In a statement accompanied by videos of the protests, the Congress youth wing said, “If Meta wants to do business in India, it must respect the Indian Constitution, not surrender to arbitrary BJP government orders.”
It had also warned Meta on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the accounts were restored.
Manu Jain, who runs the group’s social media, told the Reuters news agency on Saturday that two accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of other accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government are still restricted.
The youth wing issued a seven-day “ultimatum” to the technology giant, urging it to lift all “restrictions on opposition voices, journalists and creators”.
It asked how many Indian accounts were withheld on government orders in the past six months, and how many remain blocked. It also asked Meta to explain what it called the automated blocking of posts that mention Congress leader Rahul Gandhi or criticise Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BJP.
On Saturday, the protesters also posted a video of workers putting up a banner in central Delhi that mocked Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, as “Mark BJPberg” – suggesting that Meta favours Modi’s party.
Meta has yet to issue a statement on the matter.
Police action and BJP response
Police registered a complaint against four Youth Congress leaders in Mumbai and detained some protesters, Dainik Jagran English reported.
Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the ruling BJP, accused the protesters of vandalising Meta’s Hyderabad office and “flaunting it on social media”.
India is Meta’s biggest market by users.
In February, the government ordered platforms to remove unlawful content within three hours of notice, down from 36 hours. The government issued nearly 195,000 blocking orders to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July, the Indian Express reported.
Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025, according to its disclosures. It said most were cases in which it was “obligated to proactively restrict content” under local law.

Fernandez's lengthy excursions back ho
items.text:
Fernandez dropped, Anderson scores - Man City's £327m midfield dilemma
- Published
There may have been some eyebrows raised before kick-off when Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca decided to drop club record signing Enzo Fernandez to the bench against Fulham.
Fernandez's lengthy excursions back home to Argentina for their two fixtures during the international break may have been a factor in Maresca's thinking when selecting his starting XI for this game.
If it was, the Italian refrained from giving that as a reason. "I just think for this game it's better having Ayyoub Bouaddi in there," he told TNT Sports shortly before kick-off.
Even so, the move was a significant one as his side were in desperate need of victory after suffering three straight Premier League defeats. That winless streak extended to four after being held to a 1-1 draw.
Maresca had an opportunity to fix the issues in his set-up during the two-week break and admitted on Friday he was searching for "more balance" in the "defensive line, midfield and up front".
The pairing of the steady Bouaddi and all-action Elliot Anderson in the centre of the park was the crucial call, and it may have given Maresca some idea as to how to approach the forthcoming run of games.
"Ayyoub with Elliot were both really good," said Maresca. "Today we used Elliot a bit more attacking midfielder, he arrived inside the box and scored a fantastic goal, he had three or four moments around the box where he was really dangerous.
"It is another solution for us. In this moment, we are trying to know each other more as players and also to find the right solution."
Did Cherki's arrival restrict Anderson?
Loud jeers greeted the full-time whistle at Etihad Stadium, a culmination of the feeling that was brewing from the home supporters throughout the game.
There was a nervous tension from the beginning, which seemed to seep on to the players on the pitch.
City displayed a flat first-half performance in which they fell behind courtesy of Rodrigo Muniz's superb curling effort, and they needed a stunning second-half volley from Anderson to rescue a point.
The England international is restricted to sitting in front of the back four when Fernandez is in the side, but has the licence to roam when Bouaddi is deployed beside him.
Aside from scoring a spectacular first Premier League goal for City, Anderson created a match-high three chances and had a 100% success rate from 16 passes in the final third of the pitch.
He also had more touches in the opposition box (7), contested more duels than any other player (17) and no-one else managed to win possession back more times than him.
After dragging his side level, another marauding run into the box was snuffed out by the visiting defenders before Rayan Cherki was brought on, which meant Anderson had to retreat back down the pitch.
Maresca needed to change things in order to apply some fresh impetus in the attacking third, but the substitution of Cherki for Phil Foden seemed to limit Anderson's capabilities.
"It's not a good result, especially off the back of three losses," former City goalkeeper Joe Hart told BBC Sport. "There was some good stuff in there.
"It felt like Elliot Anderson was going to take the game by the scruff of the neck but then Cherki came on and took his position. So he [Anderson] didn't have as much of an impact on the game.
"I understood the change - when the lines are deep, there were chances of Cherki unlocking Fulham, but they just defended so well and they also offered a threat on the break."
'It is important that we find a way to keep clean sheets'
City overhauled their midfield to the tune of £327m with the signings of trio Fernandez, Anderson and Bouaddi.
The £125m club record acquisition Fernandez had made the 14,000-mile round-trip from Manchester to Buenos Aires for Argentina's friendlies against Uruguay and Costa Rica.
The trip allowed him to take the opportunity to pay a visit to boyhood club River Plate, but it is at his current club where there are question marks as to how he fits into the side.
Bouaddi's presence provides more insurance in front of the defence and the 19-year-old Moroccan has the ability to keep the ball ticking.
It means Anderson can play his natural game - but where, then, does Fernandez fit in?
The number 10 position tends to be occupied by either Cherki or Foden, while Maresca pointed out in his pre-match news conference that City "won games with Enzo and lost games with Enzo".
But the manager clearly has to work out how to get the best out of Fernandez, who was given the final five minutes against Fulham in place of Bouaddi.
"There is no point in having a brilliant squad like Manchester City if you are not going to take that into account," said Hart.
"It's very much understandable, if you're going to have a squad and you trust everyone - if someone's done the travelling, he has done the game time, you have got to expect to not use him as much."
City host Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday followed by a huge trip to Arsenal next Sunday, knowing they could head to the Emirates eight points behind the champions.
Maresca added: "For sure we don't like these kind of moments in terms of four games in a row without a win
"We also know that, unfortunately, it is normal or part of the path, you go through these kind of moments. It is important that we find a way to keep clean sheets that sometimes you need to win games 1-0 for a small difference."
Mikel Arteta's men know all about that and City now need to take a leaf out of their book.

Mexican forces arrested Chapo Isidro in Sinaloa. He was on the FBI’s most wanted list and faces US drug charges.

items.text:
Who is El Chapo Isidro, the alleged cartel boss arrested in Mexico?
Mexican forces arrested Chapo Isidro in Sinaloa. He was on the FBI’s most wanted list and faces US drug charges.
Mexican special forces have arrested Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “Chapo Isidro”, who is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, Mexico’s defence ministry said.
Meza-Flores was detained along with two other men on Friday night in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa.
The arrest comes as US President Donald Trump has been pressing Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to do more to combat drug cartels and said on Friday that Washington was working with Sheinbaum “because the cartels are running Mexico.”
“I told her that,” he said. “And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbour.”
Who is Chapo Isidro and what is he accused of?
Despite the similar nickname, Meza-Flores is not related to Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman, the jailed former leader of the Sinaloa Cartel.
Mexican authorities say Meza-Flores leads the Beltran Leyva criminal organisation and is an ally of the Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. The Mexican Secretariat of National Defence said he was wanted in Mexico on an arrest warrant for organised crime and drug offences and is subject to an extradition order to the United States.
US prosecutors first indicted Meza-Flores in 2012. In a 2019 indictment, they accused him of conspiring to manufacture and distribute cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana for the US market between 2005 and 2019. He also faces a firearms charge.
The FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in February 2025, and the US Department of State offered up to $5m for information leading to his arrest and conviction.
“Known as El Chapo Isidro, he’s accused of spending the last 20 years flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and other deadly drugs, first as an independent drug trafficker and later as the head of the Meza-Flores cartel,” said then-acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll in announcing his addition to the list.
He also said Meza-Flores and his organisation were accused of kidnapping, extortion, torture and murder.
How was Chapo Isidro arrested?
Mexico’s defence ministry said the operation followed coordination between Mexican and US intelligence agencies and involved special forces from Mexico’s National Guard and army.
Troops used “stealth and surprise” to establish a security perimeter around a house in Guasave and came under attack with gunfire and explosives before entering and arresting three men, the ministry said.
It identified the other two as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, who they identified as a financial operator. The three men were flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.
Sinaloa’s public security agency urged residents to stay indoors, avoid the area, and stay off the roads, as federal personnel had been attacked in Guasave.
The defence ministry said roadblocks were reported in four areas of Sinaloa after the arrests and that security forces were sent to reopen roads.
Videos from Guasave showed people fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as cars and petrol stations on fire, The Associated Press news agency reported.
Mexico’s security secretary, Omar Garcia Harfuch, said on Saturday that troops would remain in Sinaloa to protect residents.
“These detentions are an important step toward restoring peace in Sinaloa,” he wrote on X.

items.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
items.summary: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones s
items.text:
For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.
The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.
Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”
Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.
Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.
The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.
This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.
In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”
Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”
But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?
Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female. Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.
Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “LICENSE YOUR FACE” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.
A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”
Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”
How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.
A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”
For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.
Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.
“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”

items.title: Alcaraz defeats Shelton to reach championship match at ATP Finals
items.summary:
Carlos Alcaraz: Seven-time Grand Slam champion sinks Ben Shelton to reach championship match at ATP Finals
Carlos Alcaraz advances to the championship match at the Nitto ATP Finals for the second consecutive year; you can watch the climax to the ATP Finals in Turin this weekend on Sky Sports Tennis
items.text:
Carlos Alcaraz: Seven-time Grand Slam champion sinks Ben Shelton to reach championship match at ATP Finals
Carlos Alcaraz advances to the championship match at the Nitto ATP Finals for the second consecutive year; you can watch the climax to the ATP Finals in Turin this weekend on Sky Sports Tennis
Saturday 21 November 2026 16:05, UK
Carlos Alcaraz made it a lucky 13 wins in a row against Ben Shelton to reach Sunday's showpiece of the ATP Finals in Turin.
Alcaraz, who eased concerns about a hamstring injury by completing an unbeaten group-stage campaign, defeated American third seed Shelton 3-6 6-3 7-6 (7-1) despite heavy strapping on his upper left leg.
The Spaniard was beaten by Jannik Sinner in last year's final in Turin but will be determined to go one better this time around and claim his first year-end title. He will face either Alexander Zverev or Daniil Medvedev in Sunday's championship match.
- Keep track of the full tennis schedule live on Sky Sports
- Download Sky Sports app for analysis, news and video 📺
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW📱
Alcaraz, beaten by Shelton in a memorable US Open quarter-final clash which ended at 3.33am New York time, stretched his winning run to 13 matches after back-to-back titles in Vienna and Paris.
"I was a little bit frustrated at the beginning because I didn't start the match the way I wanted to, to be honest," Alcaraz said.
"And again, someone like Ben, big serve, big playing from the baseline, I think he just pushes you to the limit every time. I didn't start that well. And there was that break early. It was tough for me to deal with.
"But just happy that I came back in the second set playing such great tennis, step by step, focused on all my things and ended up playing good tennis.
"The third set was even closer. I think he raised the level a little bit from the second set. Myself as well. Great, great points, great games and just happy to play a great tennis in the tie-break. I think this win matters. Excited for tomorrow, and happy with everything today."
Shelton, making his second consecutive appearance in the season finale, grabbed an early break to race to a 3-0 lead.
Alcaraz, whose fitness had come under scrutiny after he left the court with heavy strapping on his left leg following Wednesday's win over Medvedev, upped his game and started moving the American around more, engaging him in longer rallies.
He earned two break points at 4-2 but could not convert either of them, with Shelton's booming serve getting him out of trouble.
The world No 4 fired a second-serve ace on his first set point to take the lead in the match, but Alcaraz kept at it and got his well-deserved break to move 5-3 up before serving out the second set.
The pair traded blows in the third set, refusing to yield serve, and took it to a tie-break where Alcaraz cruised through, sealing the win with a return winner.
Tale of the Tape
'Shelton blinked in the tie-break'
Former British No 1 Tim Henman, speaking on Sky Sports Tennis: "I thought it was a brilliant match and Shelton most definitely played his part. He made a fast start and his serving was as good as I've seen in a long time but when push came to shove in that final-set tie-break it was Shelton that blinked."
Jamie Murray said: "Shelton got off to that fast start and Carlos wasn't quite there with the energy levels and seemed so emotionally engaged in the match. He obviously brought that to the table as the match went on. In sets two and three, Alcaraz dominated on serve and it was Shelton who blinked in the tie-break."
Meanwhile, Britain's Neal Skupski and American Christian Harrison were beaten 7-6 (12-10) 6-7 (7-9) (10-7) by Marcelo Arevalo and Mate Pavic in the semi-finals of the doubles.

items.title: Grey Dawning oozes class in Betfair Chase repeat
items.summary:
Haydock: Dan Skelton's Grey Dawning oozes class in Betfair Chase repeat
The Dan Skelton-trained Grey Dawning showed his quality when defending his Betfair Chase crown at the expense of Jagwar in Haydock's National Hunt feature; the winner is now a 10-1 chance for the Ryanair Chase at the Cheltenham
items.text:
Haydock: Dan Skelton's Grey Dawning oozes class in Betfair Chase repeat
The Dan Skelton-trained Grey Dawning showed his quality when defending his Betfair Chase crown at the expense of Jagwar in Haydock's National Hunt feature; the winner is now a 10-1 chance for the Ryanair Chase at the Cheltenham Festival
Saturday 21 November 2026 16:38, UK
Grey Dawning joined an illustrious list when following up his success of 12 months ago with a smooth performance in the Betfair Chase at Haydock.
Having seen off Royale Pagaille last year, this time Dan Skelton's grey found Jagwar a tougher adversary.
Jagwar jumped with aplomb throughout for Harry Cobden, but made his first mistake at the third last which handed the initiative to Grey Dawning and Harry Skelton.
However, Jagwar came back for more and it was not until Grey Dawning showed his superior speed after the final fence the contest was over, as the 11-10 favourite went on to win by three and three-quarter lengths.
Grey Dawning joins Kauto Star, Cue Card, Bristol De Mai and Royale Pagaille to have won the Grade One back-to-back.
After returning to the winner's enclosure serenaded by chants of "walking in a Skelton wonderland" and "there's only one Harry Skelton" the jubilant brothers admitted this was a special victory.
"This is very special. Cheltenham is obviously very vast and it is hard to soak up the atmosphere but do you know what, one day when I am not riding I will always remember this place. And those are the memories you do it for," said the winning rider.
"Ups and downs you have to push through but what a special day and thank you to everyone here for making that happen. He has been a fantastic horse. He was fantastic out there today and never put a foot wrong."
The winning trainer said: "It is great to be involved in such iconic horses and it is just an amazing achievement from the horse and a fabulous ride from Harry. It feels like a real team atmosphere and it's great.
"Harry is riding at the top of his game and he does more for me than you will ever appreciate and it is a fantastic team effort. Me and Harry are the strikers if you like but it is our job to help everybody along."
Grey Dawning finished a highly creditable fourth to Gaelic Warrior in the Gold Cup last season before landing the Melling Chase on his final start at Aintree and the champion trainer is inclined to leave the blue riband to others this time round.
"Of course the Gold Cup is our ultimate test in the sport but we tried that. I thought we had him in Gold Cup form and so it turned out. If he hadn't been in great form he wouldn't have been able to do what he did at Aintree," said Dan Skelton.
"The truth is we tried for a Gold Cup and we weren't quite good enough. The Ryanair is a Grade One, it is the marquee race on the Thursday and this horse is definitely better in a Ryanair than a Gold Cup and that's where he will go."
Skelton went on to say he would enter the horse in the King George "in case it is abandoned and we got it left-handed somewhere" as well as Leopardstown at Christmas.

items.title: US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?
items.summary:
US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?
What happens between the US midterm elections and January, when Democrats take control of Congress?
The United States midterm elections are over, and the Democrats have won control of both houses of Congress. However, they do not t
items.text:
US midterms 2026: What happens before the new Congress takes office?
What happens between the US midterm elections and January, when Democrats take control of Congress?
The United States midterm elections are over, and the Democrats have won control of both houses of Congress. However, they do not take power until January.
Election officials are still certifying results, while the newly elected lawmakers are preparing to take office, and the outgoing Congress is continuing its legislative work.
So what happens between now and January, and what will change as the 120th Congress takes office?
What has happened so far?
After the elections, officials have been finalising the results and completing the certification process, which varies by state.
On November 9, the existing Congress returned to Washington for what is known as the “lame-duck” session.
A lame-duck session occurs when Congress meets after an election but before the new Congress takes office.
This means the Republicans still have the majority in both chambers of Congress and can continue passing legislation until the new Congress takes office in January.
November-December: New lawmakers prepare to take office
During this time, newly elected members start preparing to take office in January.
They attend orientation sessions in Washington, hire staff, and learn more about how Congress operates day-to-day.
Political parties also choose their leaders in the House of Representatives and the Senate. The party controlling each chamber selects the majority leader, while the other party selects the minority leader. The House will also vote on a speaker, who leads the House leadership.
The Republican Party has already re-elected John Thune as its Senate leader, entering the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency.
The election on the Democratic side, however, is shaping up to be more of a fight.
Among Democrats, Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Senator and current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York to be Senate majority leader, with a vote scheduled for December 1.
Speaking on Al Jazeera’s This Is America, Democratic strategist Roger Fisk suggested that the differences between the two candidates may be more about their methods than their political goals.
“I think the difference would probably come in the how rather than the what,” Fisk said.
Republican strategist Doug Heye said the leadership debate reflects wider questions facing both parties after the midterms.
“Both parties have somewhat of an identity crisis,” he said, referring to the Republicans’ losses and the future of the party but also the divisions in the Democratic Party between moderate Democrats and more progressive ones.
December 11: A government funding deadline
One of the biggest challenges of the current Congress is a December 11 deadline to approve government funding.
Congress passed a temporary spending bill, known as a continuing resolution, to keep the federal agencies functioning without approving a full-year budget.
But before the measure expires, Congress must approve another bill to keep the government funded.
If lawmakers do not reach a deal, part of the federal government could face a shutdown.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Heye suggested a temporary funding extension could push negotiations into February, by which time Democrats will control both chambers.
“So that would probably go through February,” he said, referring to a possible continuing resolution.
Heye also said the federal debt ceiling is another challenge for the new Congress.
“These are two things that never come up on the campaign trail, but it can be very important to tell us about the next two years,” he added.
December 17-18: Congress wraps up
The current Congress is expected to finalise its legislative work before the Christmas holidays.
The House’s final sitting day is planned for December 17 and the Senate’s for December 18.
But lawmakers could remain in Washington longer if major issues remain unresolved.
Even if lawmakers finish their work earlier, the 119th Congress’s term does not officially end until January 3.
January 3, 2027: The new Congress takes power
The 120th Congress starts its term at noon (17:00 GMT) on January 3, 2027.
But January 3 falls on a Sunday, and Congress could pass a law setting a different date for the first meeting.
When the new House convenes, lawmakers must elect a Speaker before being sworn in. Newly elected senators will also take their oaths.
With Democrats controlling both chambers, they will gain authority over congressional committees, legislative priorities and investigations into the administration of President Donald Trump.
“You’re going to have in the House and the Senate something called committee chairs, and they’re all going to be Democrats, and they’re all going to have subpoena power,” Heye told Al Jazeera.
However, he warned that congressional investigations could complicate negotiations between Democrats and the White House.
What changes politically in January?
Trump will remain president after the midterms, but he will face a Congress controlled by Democrats in both chambers.
This means his administration will have to negotiate with the Democrats to pass legislation, while a Democrat-led Senate will control the confirmation process for presidential nominees.
Democrats will also be able to launch congressional investigations and hold hearings looking at the president’s actions and the actions of those in his inner circle and administration.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has already outlined some of the party’s priorities.
“We need to end the war of choice in Iran. We need to stop the Trump tariffs,” he said.
He also called for reversing Medicaid and food assistance cuts and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.

items.text:
EU and Indonesia sign landmark trade deal
November 21, 2026
The European Union and Indonesia signed a free trade deal on Saturday, describing it as a new chapter in economic relations between the two sides.
"This is one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia," Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said at the signing ceremony on Saturday.
"Together, we represent a market of 730 million people," she added.
The Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and the additional Investment Protection Agreement (IPA) are designed to reduce trade barriers and attract investment in strategic sectors such as electric vehicles, electronics, and pharmaceuticals.
The agreement comes after almost 10 years of negotiations and is part of a wider series of trade deals by the EU.
'Keeping the doors open when others are closing theirs'
The bloc hopes to reduce its reliance on individual economic partners as trade with both China and the US has become more difficult in recent years.
Von der Leyen also stressed the importance of international cooperation, saying that "in a time when others are closing their doors, we keep ours open."
The deal sees tariffs on about 98% of EU exports to Indonesia to be done away with. The EU estimates that European companies could save more than €600 million (around €658 million) per year.
"The benefits for our exporters are concrete and measurable," Indonesian Minister of Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto said, hailing a "new chapter" in economic relations with the EU. He said the deal would benefit his country’s main exports to Europe, including palm oil, footwear and textiles.
Palm oil and deforestation had been major stumbling blocks during the negotiations, and the agreement includes mechanisms for cooperation on regulatory and sustainability issues as well as a dedicated protocol on palm oil to address environmental concerns.
The EU parliament is now expected to greenlight the deal while Indonesian authorities will also complete the ratification process so it can enter into force in 2027.

items.text:
Diallo present as Africa’s Motsepe reiterates support for FIFA’s Infantino
Africa’s CAF join South America’s CONMEBOL in giving unanimous support of FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s re-election.
African football supremo Patrice Motsepe has said that all 54 members of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) support Gianni Infantino’s bid for re-election as FIFA president.
Motsepe made the declaration on Saturday in Abuja, where CAF is holding its ordinary general assembly and at which one of Infantino’s two rivals, French football chief Philippe Diallo, is present.
Former Japan Football Association president Kozo Tashima is the other candidate.
The trio will learn whether they have been successful on March 18 next year in Rabat – the winning candidate must obtain a majority of the 211 associations.
CAF’s support for Infantino comes hours after another of his steadfast supporters, South American football’s governing body CONMEBOL, gave him their “unanimous” backing.
CAF has been consistently behind Infantino – who is seeking a fourth and final term – even after the furore he stirred up in July with his short-lived FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.
Morocco is cohosting the 2030 World Cup.
“Gianni, you have our support on behalf of the 54 nations in Africa to be our candidate,” Motsepe said.
“I have a report from all 54 member associations in Africa to say that we are unanimously supporting Gianni.”
Infantino has faced multiple calls to step down and lost the backing of European football’s governing body UEFA, while CONCACAF has also been strident in its criticism of the 56-year-old Swiss lawyer.
Motsepe, though, has been a vocal supporter, and Infantino said such loyalty was reciprocal.
“You will always find, in me and in FIFA, a trusted partner,” Infantino told the assembly, announcing cash inflow of $25m to each member of CAF, starting January 2027 for development projects.
On Wednesday, UEFA Vice President Laura McAllister told the AFP news agency that Diallo, a 63-year-old lawyer whose Senegalese-born father boxed for France at the 1960 Olympics in Rome, should not be seen as solely a European candidate.
“He is a Francophone, which is an important asset in lots of CAF countries,” she said.
McAllister, who in 2023 became the first woman to be elected a vice president of UEFA, noted that confederations do not vote as a bloc.
“There is a soft space which Philippe can exploit and convince some federations within each confederation to support a reform agenda,” the 61-year-old said.
“There is a lot of discomfort around the behaviour of Gianni Infantino and a desire to challenge the concentration of power in his hands.
“This applies everywhere in world football. This is not about Europe; the same rules apply globally.”

items.title: VAR review: Should Haaland's goal vs Fulham have been disallowed?
items.summary:
The video assistant referee causes controversy every week, whether it be the Premier League, Champions League or FA Cup, but how are those decisions made and are they correct?
For the 2026-27 season, we are taking a look at the major incidents to explain the process in terms of both VAR protocol and
items.text:
The video assistant referee causes controversy every week, whether it be the Premier League, Champions League or FA Cup, but how are those decisions made and are they correct?
For the 2026-27 season, we are taking a look at the major incidents to explain the process in terms of both VAR protocol and the laws of the game. The most surprising, controversial and complicated decisions will be examined all season long right here.
Photo credit: USA Sports, NBC
Andy Davies (@andydaviesref) is a former Select Group referee, with over 12 seasons on the elite list, working across the Premier League and Championship. With extensive experience at the elite level, he has operated within the VAR space in the Premier League and offers a unique insight into the processes, rationale and protocols that are delivered on a matchday.
Haaland goal vs. Fulham ruled out
Man City vs. Fulham (Nov. 21)
Referee: Tom Bramall
VAR: James Bell
Time: 24 minutes
Incident: Man City's Erling Haaland disallowed goal for foul on Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno.
What Happened: Haaland managed to get on the end of a deep cross, directing the ball into arms of Leno. However, the Fulham goalkeeper appeared to spill the ball, and Haaland followed up his original effort and bundled the ball into the net. Referee Bramall disallowed the goal as he felt Leno had control of the ball, awarding a foul to Fulham.
VAR Decision: No goal, stuck with the referee's on-field decision.
ELLIOT ANDERSON LEVELS IT WITH HIS FIRST FOR MAN CITY 🚨 A header is cleared out of the box, but Anderson fires through a crowd of players to bring Manchester City level against Fulham! 🔵 Manchester City: 1 🔴 Fulham: 1 ⏱️ 57' https://t.co/UPiNHMym3a
— USA Sports (@usasports) November 21, 2026
VAR Review: A debatable outcome, where there is no conclusive evidence to prove the on-field decision incorrect, and therefore this is not an incident VAR would intervene on.
Verdict / Insight: By the laws of the game, the goalkeeper only needs to have one hand engaged with the ball for it to be deemed to be under his control.
Referee Tom Bramall had a poor view of the challenge and its circumstance. In truth, he would have used a level of experience and guesswork to reach his outcome of disallowing the goal, and it would have felt the best outcome in the moment -- I would have given the same!
However, whilst I have seen some "still" images that possibly show the goalkeeper's hands near the ball, replays show a slightly different picture where the ball looked to have been spilt by the Fulham goalkeeper and equally his immediate body language in real-time and before he had time to think for a second, told a story of a player who had made an error.
Ultimately, Fulham's Leno can think himself fortunate that this one fell his way and City can be aggrieved; it's a decision that could have fallen either way in real time.
Did Lammens interfere with Suzuki?
Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa (Nov. 8)
Referee: Chris Kavanagh
VAR: Craig Pawson
Time: 96 minutes
Incident: Possible foul in Manchester United's equalizing goal.
What happened: Bruno Fernandes swung in a last-chance corner kick as Man United threw every player they had on the pitch, including keeper Senne Lammens, into the penalty area at 4-3 down.
Patrick Dorgu outjumped the Aston Villa defenders and, with keeper Zion Suzuki flapping at the ball, nodded home what seemed like a straightforward header into the net. However, Suzuki believed he was fouled by opposite number Lammens as the United No. 1 attempted to block the Villa keeper. Lammens made contact with Suzuki while neither looking at the ball nor making any attempt to play it.
Referee Kavanagh was unmoved by the appeals, yellow-carding Suzuki for his protests and awarding the goal.
VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of goal.
VAR review: VAR checked the incident and was comfortable that although Lammens clearly had intent to disturb Suzuki from having a clear path to punch the ball away by bumping into him, any contact was minimal and, more importantly, his impact on the Villa keeper was a 50-50 call.
This is a ratio where VAR is not keen to get involved and will stick with the on-field decision.
Didn't notice in real time but that is literally VAR's job and it gets no better with every viewing. If that was on Lammens we'd be fuming so got to be honest we got away with one there
— Mark Goldbridge (@markgoldbridge) November 8, 2026
Verdict: Even prominent Man United fan Mark Goldbridge was sure that VAR should have got involved. But I believe the VAR was correct not to intervene in this situation as it fell short of the threshold for a clear on-field error.
Though Lammens' intention was obvious, intent is not a punishable offense, and the many replays didn't show enough of an impactful physical action on Suzuki that met the criteria for an intervention. However, Lammens did gamble with this play, and if referee Kavanagh had judged his action differently and awarded a late free kick to Villa, United could have few complaints.
This was a borderline call either way, and I am comfortable that the on-field decision should stick regardless of which way it fell.
Arsenal robbed of a penalty
Arsenal 1-0 Hull City (Nov. 7)
Referee: Farai Hallam
VAR: Michael Oliver
Time: 42 minutes
Incident: Penalty not awarded to Arsenal for an offside offense.
What happened: Hull's Nobel Mendy appeared to grab the shirt of Kai Havertz as the Arsenal attacker attempted to get on the end of a ball into the box.
In a confusing twist and following a VAR review, Hallam explained to the stadium that a foul action had been committed by Mendy, but Havertz was in an offside position and therefore the decision was no penalty and a restart of an indirect free kick to Hull.
VAR decision: VAR recommended an on-field review for a possible penalty to Arsenal.

items.title: Chesang calls for probe into ethnic tensions in Trans Nzoia, accuses Natembeya of incitement
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 21 – Trans Nzoia Senator Allan Chesang has called on security agencies and the National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC) to investigate rising ethnic tensions in the county, accusing Governor George Natembeya of making inflammatory remarks and mobilising groups to targe
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 21 – Trans Nzoia Senator Allan Chesang has called on security agencies and the National Cohesion and Integration Commission (NCIC) to investigate rising ethnic tensions in the county, accusing Governor George Natembeya of making inflammatory remarks and mobilising groups to target political opponents.
Chesang warned that escalating political hostilities risk undermining peace and economic activity in the county, which is one of Kenya’s major food-producing regions.
Addressing the media, the senator also condemned the attack on blogger Amos Masika, popularly known as Hammer Hammer , saying the incident should be investigated without being turned into a political contest.
He accused some county leaders of rushing to assign political responsibility for the attack before investigations by the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) had established what happened.
“Instead of concentrating on finding out what really happened to our brother Hamma, who has a young family, it is deeply painful that we are skipping straight to political motives,” Chesang said.
He argued that investigators should consider all possible motives, including business disputes and personal differences, rather than prematurely attributing the incident to political rivalry.
The senator said leaders should allow the DCI to establish the circumstances surrounding the attack and warned against making public accusations that could inflame tensions among communities.
Chesang particularly criticised Natembeya for allegedly introducing ethnic divisions into the matter, insisting that Trans Nzoia had traditionally enjoyed peaceful relations among its diverse communities.
“Trans Nzoia is a cosmopolitan area and we have always enjoyed peace,” he said, citing intermarriage and coexistence among Luhya, Kalenjin, Kikuyu and Teso communities.
He accused the governor of making statements that could pit communities against each other and urged political leaders to stop using tribal identity to advance political differences.
The senator also questioned the state of healthcare services in the county, saying Masika had to be transferred to Eldoret in neighbouring Uasin Gishu County after he failed to receive the required emergency treatment locally.
“Our county hospital has no medication and lacks proper services, forcing us to seek emergency care in a neighbouring county and rush your own staff member to Eldoret,” Chesang said.
He challenged the county administration to prioritise healthcare delivery, arguing that the incident had exposed weaknesses in local medical facilities.
Chesang further accused Natembeya’s personal lawyer, whom he identified as Achesa, of spreading propaganda over the case instead of allowing investigations and court processes to take their course.
He questioned claims allegedly linking him to the handling of suspects in another case, asking what authority a senator would have to direct the DCI on where suspects should be charged.
The senator also warned that political tensions were affecting businesses and livelihoods, saying traders and residents were becoming uncomfortable conducting business in the county.
“Trans Nzoia is the breadbasket of Kenya, so let us focus on feeding the nation,” he said, adding that market traders were increasingly being drawn into political disagreements.
He called on residents to reject violence and urged leaders to stop using young people and bloggers to advance political rivalries.
Chesang said that if investigations established that Masika was attacked because of political differences, Natembeya would bear responsibility, citing the alleged use of the county communication team to attack political opponents online.
The Transnzoia governor urged security agencies and the NCIC to investigate what he described as political incitement, warning that failure to address the tensions could trigger wider conflict.

Khiara Keating’s resilient performance in goal denied Chelsea, the Women’s Super League leaders, and earned Liverpool a point. After hard-fought 1-0 wins against Manchester City last Saturday and Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday night, Chelsea drew a blank.
Against Gareth Taylor’s side, Chelsea’s la
items.text:
Khiara Keating’s resilient performance in goal denied Chelsea, the Women’s Super League leaders, and earned Liverpool a point. After hard-fought 1-0 wins against Manchester City last Saturday and Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday night, Chelsea drew a blank.
Against Gareth Taylor’s side, Chelsea’s lack of cutting edge was clear a week after beating City to go top. The calf injury picked up by Melvine Malard against City, the absence of Lauren James, who has a thigh injury, and the form of Aggie Beever-Jones, who scored her first WSL goal in more than a year in the 6-0 defeat of Charlton, have left Chelsea’s attack short.
Despite almost 70% possession and 47 touches in the box to Liverpool’s 12, Sonia Bompastor’s side amassed only 19 shots to Liverpool’s 13 and seven on target to their opponents’ four. Although the Blues remain unbeaten in the WSL, their third draw in five games in all competitions means City can leapfrog them at the top if they beat Tottenham on Sunday.
Liverpool had chances, particularly in the first half, but were hanging on after the break and Keating helped them to a fourth clean sheet, a tally bettered only by Bompastor’s side.
“It was a bit stressful; we don’t want to sit back but in games like this you have to ride it out,” Keating told Sky Sports. “A clean sheet is always on our minds every game. We knew the mission. It was such a close game, it could have gone either way.”
The January transfer window will give the Blues an opportunity to strengthen their attack, but with three games before the winter break they need to step up in the final third, starting with their tricky fixture against London City Lionesses on 12 December after the international break.
- This story will be updated after London City Lionesses v Crystal Palace

items.summary:

British maritime agency reports two incidents near Oman, while Iran says a tanker caught fire due to naval mine.
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Stra
items.text:
Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as Iran tightens grip on shipping
British maritime agency reports two incidents near Oman, while Iran says a tanker caught fire due to naval mine.
British maritime authorities have reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran continues to restrict shipping through the vital waterway.
The incidents were reported on Saturday near Oman, amid a war involving Tehran, Washington and Tel Aviv that began with the United States and Israel attacking Iran in late February.
Tehran has since sought to tighten its control over the strait, which carried nearly a fifth of the world’s crude oil supplies before the conflict.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre, a British agency that monitors threats to commercial shipping, said one tanker was hit at its rear about 20km (13 miles) north of Khasab, a port town on Oman’s northern coast.
Another tanker was struck in its engine room about 31km (20 miles) east of Khasab, the agency said.
No casualties were reported, but it remained unclear whether the two incidents involved separate vessels.
Iran’s navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait.
In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off.
The Iranian account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was involved in either incident reported by UKMTO.
A ‘pattern’
Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week.
Citing statements issued by Iran’s armed forces, Serdar said about 25 incidents had been reported since the previous Saturday, averaging roughly three a day, a trend he called “quite dramatic”.
“This is becoming a pattern,” Serdar said, explaining that “Iranians are saying the Strait of Hormuz is under their control; that any ship that is passing through the Strait of Hormuz has to be in full coordination with the Iranian authorities and must follow the roads and the lanes that are determined by Iran.”
If ships do not comply, Iran says “they are either going to be attacked, or they are going to hit the sea mines that are laid by the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC or the Iranian forces”, Serdar added.
Our correspondent said Tehran was deliberately escalating tensions to send a message that if Iran could not export its oil, other countries would not be able to do so either.
He said Iran was also seeking to show that it remained in control of the strait, a narrow passage connecting the Gulf with international shipping routes.
The US has responded to Iran’s restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway.
The confrontation has raised concerns over the security of a major route for global energy supplies, with commercial vessels caught in the struggle between Washington and Tehran over access to the strait.

Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
The Anthropic IPO raises big questions about the future of AI, the company’s safety-first missi
items.text:
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.
Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
The Anthropic IPO raises big questions about the future of AI, the company’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism.
The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.
All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.
You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder.
Thanks. Great to be here.
I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos.
I know.
It’s like a normal thing that happened.
It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.
[Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.
Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.
Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”
What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?
I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.
But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.
I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.
So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.
Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?
Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.
Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. items.text:
Punchestown: Champion Hurdle heroine Lossiemouth imperious in Morgiana repeat
Champion Hurdle heroine Lossiemouth got her 2026/27 campaign off to the best possible start, leading from pillar to post to defend her Morgiana Hurdle title at Punchestown for Willie Mullins and Paul Townend
Saturday 21 November 2026 15:58, UK
Lossiemouth made every yard of the running as she coasted to victory to make it back-to-back wins in the William Hill Morgiana Hurdle at Punchestown.
The seven-year-old started out on the tried-and-tested route to the Champion Hurdle and barely had to break sweat as she cantered to an 11-length victory.
She had the field under pressure three furlongs out as she streaked clear and while William Munny tried to keep tabs on her, he was the first horse beaten as he weakened markedly with the race taking shape as Paul Townend kept the 1-6 favourite up to her work.
It was left to Noel Meade's Blake to chase home the current champion hurdler.
Mullins said: "I was very pleased with her. I think she was a lot fitter than I thought she was. I was really pleased how she jumped the fifth last and the fourth last. She put in two tremendous jumps at those and I thought that might take a lot out of her.
"Paul said she didn't even take a blow, she just galloped on the whole way. He was very pleased with her and so was I.
"She's just a real genuine mare. I'm happy that I left off the cheekpieces today. I don't think she needs them all the time. She's back in two-mile racing mode now. She was in sort of staying racing mode before that. Now that she's running in two-mile races all the time she's sharper.
"I'd imagine it's the same road from here - Christmas, Dublin Racing Festival and on to Cheltenham then."
Coral left Lossiemouth unchanged as the 5-4 favourite for the Champion Hurdle.

Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on big tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised
items.text:
New EU budget proposal aims at tax gobal tech giants
November 21, 2026
European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a new draft for the next EU budget.
Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on big tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.
The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.
A first draft for the 2028 to 2034 budget was proposed by the EU Commission in 2025 but was criticised, especially by a group of northern European members including Germany who wanted the budget to be much smaller.
Following that criticism, the European Council President has now suggested a new draft, which is smaller by €204 billion.
But divisions among member states appear to remain, with France immediately coming out against Costa’s new draft, saying it was "deeply disappointing."
What’s the plan for the tech tax?
The proposal includes a string of new "revenue channels," explicitly intended to "to keep national contributions at a reasonable level," so that member state will have to contribute less than otherwise would be the case.
The biggest splash would likely come from a tax on companies with an annual turnover from digital activities of at least 50 million euros in the EU and 750 million euros worldwide.
Those firms would be subject to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data," according to Costa.
Aside from the tech tax, the "balanced basket of new own resources" also includes taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste.
What happens next?
Neither the EU Commission nor European Council President Costa will have the final word on the budget. Costa's plan will now be at the centre of hours of talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.
"This is a realistic budget that addresses our new priorities while preserving our established policies," Costa wrote about his proposal. "I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement."
But an initial reaction from France suggests that any final agreement might still be some way off.
The French presidency said the budget "falls well short of what is needed, particularly on the Common Agricultural Policy, notably to guarantee income support for farmers."
"As it stands, this proposal from the President of the European Council does not provide a basis for an agreement."
The EU was hoping to reach a general agreement on the budget by the end of 2026 with its formal adoption planned for 2027.

items.text:
Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
- Published
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run more than 24 hours into overtime as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
This still remains the main sticking point, along with a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not in sight.
Not all countries have the funding or capacity to do this, and at some point the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.
This means the summit would end with no deal and have to be suspended. This has only happened once before in the 24 years countries have been meeting.
- More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged 
  - Published1 day ago
Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.
Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas, external.
The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.
Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.
The 'worst' COP ever?
It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.
This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - that has now been removed.
"We did not come here to beg we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.
These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected" said one observer.
