QPR get first away win since August at 10-man Millwall
Cyle Larin returned to action with a bang as Southampton extended their unbeaten run at home in the Championship to 18 games
items.text:
Championship roundup: Southampton get Larin lift as Norwich win five in a row
Southampton 2-0 Derby; Norwich 2-1 Cardiff
QPR get first away win since August at 10-man Millwall
Cyle Larin returned to action with a bang as Southampton extended their unbeaten run at home in the Championship to 18 games with a 2-0 victory over second-bottom Derby.
Larin turned in his eighth goal of the season but his first since 12 September – after a four-game drought and a hamstring problem. Divin Mubama added a second in stoppage time as Saints shrugged off worries of failing against lower-placed sides – having dropped points against Watford, Preston, Wrexham, Lincoln and Bolton already this season.
But for their four-point deduction for Spygate, the result would have taken Southampton top for at least a couple of hours. Derby would wind up bottom if Preston pulled off an unlikely win at West Ham.
Norwich came from behind to beat Cardiff 2-1 and make it five straight Championship victories – after losing their previous five. The Canaries went behind just after the break when Yousef Salech got on the end of a free-kick from deep but the visitors were quickly back on level terms as Paris Maghoma scored for the fourth game running.
Mathias Kvistgaarden then tapped home in the 68th minute after his penalty had been kept out by Nathan Trott. Ronan Kpakio had been penalised for bringing down Andre Brooks. Cardiff performed gamely all afternoon but were unable to get the equaliser their gutsy performance probably deserved.
Nicolas Madsen’s scruffy winner gave Queens Park Rangers their first away victory since August as they defeated Millwall 1-0 at the Den. The result against their London rivals ensured the Hoops will end the weekend inside the playoff places after they played the majority of the contest against 10 men following Zak Sturge’s 15th-minute red card. Sturge was shown a straight red card for tripping Paul Smyth just outside the area as the last defender.
QPR took the lead in first-half stoppage time as Lukas Jensen first saved from Ilias Chair before Madsen’s follow-up crossed the line despite Caleb Taylor’s attempted heroics. Despite a commendable defensive performance with depleted numbers, this was a third straight defeat for Millwall whose campaign continues to stutter.
Later kick-offs include Birmingham, the leaders, at Stoke, Middlesbrough in second at home to Bristol City and third-placed Wolves hosting Charlton.

items.text:
Russia strikes Zelenskyy's hometown, killing 2
November 21, 2026
Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.
The attacks come amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine, on three occasions this week, struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had vowed a "painful" response to the Kerch attack, as the bridge is vital for war supplies for Russian forces in the south.
What do we know?
Among the dead in Friday evening's double-tap strikes on Kryvyi Rih were a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while several children were among the 60 wounded, the Ukrainian officials said.
Several fires broke out and damage was caused to about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram.
Moscow, meanwhile, confirmed a further strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih.
Russia's Defense Ministry said a thermal power plant in the city was hit, along with a power substation in the region of Rivne, on the opposite side of the country.
Both facilities supply electricity to the industry supporting Ukraine's military, the ministry added.
What are the other latest developments?
Elsewhere in the nearly five-year-long war, Russia also struck a cargo vessel near Odesa, which Moscow said was carrying dual-use goods for the Ukrainian military.
Eleven people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday.
One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.
In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.
Finland, meanwhile, said it detected a drone attack on Saturday morning on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, prompting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the war is "spilling over into our immediate vicinity."
After damage to Russia's Kerch bridge to Crimea, Zelenskyy warned in an interview with US broadcaster NBC that the structure "will not remain standing anyway."

items.text:
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
Joint statement by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.
On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.
We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.
Our rationale is outlined below.
The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, part of the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.
- The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.
- Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures.
- 
The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools (comparator and con-leche –compare), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis.
- 
The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/. These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.
Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.
We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

items.text:
Man City claw back 1-1 draw with Fulham to end three-game losing streak
Rodrigo Muniz set Fulham on the way but Elliot Anderson volley earns Manchester City a valuable Premier League point.
Manchester City avoided the ignominy of a fourth-straight defeat as Elliot Anderson’s strike kept an unsettled Etihad Stadium at bay in a 1-1 draw with Fulham in the Premier League.
Rodrigo Muniz opened the scoring in the 16th minute for the away side, who had only won two of their opening 10 league games to start the day just two points and three places above the relegation zone.
Anderson’s driven volley in the 57th minute handed City their first point in the league since they opened their campaign with seven consecutive wins.
The midfielder, who had netted his first City goal since arriving from Nottingham Forest, nearly added a second with a burst into the box, but dragged his effort across the face.
City, who sit five points off top spot, had lost to Brighton, RB Leipzig and Forest in their previous games.
Holders, and league leaders Arsenal play their game in hand over City at Newcastle later on Saturday.
More to follow.

items.title: Elliot Anderson ends Manchester City’s losing run but boos greet Fulham draw
items.summary: Manchester City are living in Premier League purgatory, without a win in four but at least ended their three-game losing run against Fulham. As they await the fate of their much-publicised appeal after being found guilty of financial breaches, their form has slumped as further evidenced by a passive
items.text:
Manchester City are living in Premier League purgatory, without a win in four but at least ended their three-game losing run against Fulham. As they await the fate of their much-publicised appeal after being found guilty of financial breaches, their form has slumped as further evidenced by a passive draw.
Arguments will be made over Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal but City did not deserve anything more. The Norwegian uncharacteristically missed a number of fine chances as Rodrigo Muniz took advantage of City’s porous defence, who had to rely on Elliot Anderson to get anything out of the fixture.
City approached the game with the same subdued nature of the crowd, as is customary for a Saturday lunchtime kick-off. For a team amid a poor run of domestic form, they offered little in the way of dynamism from the off. A couple of harsh chances were brushed off by Fulham, who were allowed to ease themselves into the game.
Confusion between defence and midfield has repeatedly caused problems for City under Enzo Maresca, who witnessed Marc Guéhi going over the halfway to press a throw-in deep inside the Fulham half. When the visitors won the first head, the centre-back was out of position and everything was far too simple from then on. The former City winger Oscar Bobb shimmied and Muniz curled into the top corner from the edge of the box, before an emotional celebration in honour of his pregnant wife, who previously suffered a miscarriage.
It was a day where the team needed to inspire the crowd and City finally discovered intent midway through the first-half. Iliman Ndiaye’s dangerous cross found Haaland at the back post but he could not finish at the first time of asking, allowing Bernd Leno to get his hands to the ball but whether the German had it under control is another matter. Haaland jabbed at the goalkeeper, nudging the ball through his grasp but the referee signalled fouled and no one with access to replays disagreed. No one connected to City felt it was a correct decision, with Thomas Bramall offering the benefit of the doubt to Leno.
City lacked a cutting edge; Phil Foden, given the nod over Rayan Cherki at No 10, had chances to feed Haaland in good positions but twice the execution of the pass ensured there was no change. At the third time of asking, the pair connected, only for Haaland to balloon at shot from close range, and under little pressure, into the stands. Every Haaland finish was a whimsical version of what everyone expects, miscuing a straightforward chance from a Nico O’Reilly cross, too. It felt like one of those days.
City continued to find it difficult as David Affengruber and Calvin Bassey put in fine performances at centre-back, reading every strand of danger and snuffing it out. To find a way back into the match, City needed to increase the tempo and find the absent aggressive, something Anderson obliged by violently volleying a cleared corner into the bottom corner from 18 yards.
Anderson is becoming Maresca’s most trusted player, preferred to Enzo Fernández to provide the thrust alongside Ayyoub Bouaddi. In a team lacking energy, the England international is a catalyst in what is a difficult period for an underperforming team. He latched onto a Haaland flick-on in each of a second but could not stay on his feet. The pair combined for a second time but Anderson’s quick feet and cute finish concluded with the ball slipping an inch wide.
With the tide turning, City’s flaws were there for all to see as Fulham won the ball and within a blink of an eye Muniz was through on goal thanks to the lack of resistance in blue. Gianluigi Donnarumma was the last – and sturdiest – line of defence, repeating the feat against Bassey soon after. These were the best chances of the second half, as City were unable to create a meaningful chance on another worrying afternoon, which concluded with further jeers.

items.title: Elon Musk’s lawyer joining Tom Brady in buying Chelsea stake
items.summary: Elon Musk’s lawyer is joining Tom Brady in buying a stake in Chelsea. The Guardian revealed on Friday that the NFL player is in discussions about purchasing a minority shareholding at Stamford Bridge and can now disclose that Alex Spiro of the New York law firm Quinn Emmanuel is also seeking to buy
items.text:
Elon Musk’s lawyer is joining Tom Brady in buying a stake in Chelsea. The Guardian revealed on Friday that the NFL player is in discussions about purchasing a minority shareholding at Stamford Bridge and can now disclose that Alex Spiro of the New York law firm Quinn Emmanuel is also seeking to buy a stake by investing in Chelsea’s majority owners, Clearlake Capital.
Brady and Spiro, who is representing planned Fifa investor Joshua Kushner in a legal battle against Uefa, would become limited partners in Clearlake with no voting rights at Chelsea if the transactions are completed.
Clearlake have been seeking additional investors since agreeing to buy the shares of former partners Todd Boehly and Mark Walter for around £1bn in September, a deal that is due to be completed by the end of the year.
Clearlake will own 86.5% of Chelsea after buying out Boehly and Walter, who both held stakes of 12.9%, with the proposed investments of Brady and Spiro understood to be considerably smaller. As part of that transaction Boehly and Walter’s partner, the Swiss philanthropist Hansjorg Wyss, chose to stay at Chelsea by buying 12.9% of Clearlake’s shareholding.
Any other future investors such as Brady and Spiro would follow the same model.
Spiro has represented Musk since 2018 and advised on his $44bn (£33.6bn) purchase of Twitter (now X) in 2022, as well as working for other celebrity clients, including Alec Baldwin, Kim Kardashian and Jay-Z.
In 2019 he successfully defended Musk in a notorious defamation trial relating to comments he made about the rescuer of junior football players from a Thailand cave, while in 2024 his defence helped Baldwin’s acquittal on charges involuntary manslaughter after a cinematographer died on the set of his film Rust, when a prop revolver discharged a live round.
Last summer Spiro was also appointed to represent Kushner, whose company Thrive Capital were the lead investors in Gianni Infantino’s $4.2bn World Cup sell-off scheme, in a legal challenge from Uefa.
Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared, is facing court claims in the United States from Uefa’s lawyers to disclose all communications relating to Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise plan. Last week a New York court rejected a motion by two Fifa subsidiaries to dismiss Uefa’s claim, but the courts have yet to rule on the disclosure filing.
Brady owned a 3.3% stake in Championship club Birmingham City until earlier this month, with sources involved in his decision to sell those shares telling the Guardian that he was paving the way to invest in Chelsea.
The seven-time Super Bowl winner was a guest of Chelsea when they won the Club World Cup in New Jersey last year, and has a good relationship with the Clearlake’s main power broker, Behdad Eghbali, who has led discussions on behalf of the club.
Brady bought into Birmingham in August 2023, less than a year after his second and final retirement from the NFL, following the club’s takeover by Tom Wagner’s Knighthead Capital.
The 49-year-old was appointed chair of the club’s advisory board and had a prominent role in the 2025 Amazon Prime documentary Built in Birmingham: Brady & The Blues, which made headlines when he questioned the “work ethic” of Wayne Rooney, who was the manager. Brady also owns a minority stake in the NFL team the Las Vegas Raiders, which he bought alongside Wagner.
Chelsea declined to comment.

Norwich 2-1 Cardiff: Canaries hit back for victory
Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Norwich City and Cardiff City at Carrow Road on Saturday; Paris Maghoma and Mathias Kvistgaarden net as Canaries secure comeback win.
Saturday 21 November 2026 14:40, UK
Norwich came from behind to beat Cardiff 2-1 and make it five straight Championship victories - after losing their previous five.
The Canaries went behind just after the break when Yousef Salech got on the end of a free-kick from deep but the visitors were quickly back on level terms as Paris Maghoma scored for the fourth game running.
And it did not take them long to score what proved to be the winner, with Mathias Kvistgaarden tapping home on 68 minutes after his penalty had been kept out by Nathan Trott.
Cardiff performed gamely all afternoon but were unable to get the equaliser their gutsy performance probably deserved.
Both sides knocked the ball around neatly in an evenly-contested first half, with the visitors creating the better chances.
With just three minutes on the clock home keeper Dan Grimshaw did well to tip a beautifully-struck Rubin Colwill free-kick over while the Cardiff skipper went even closer midway through the half. This time a move that ran the length of the pitch ended with the big midfielder clipping the crossbar with an effort from just outside the 'D'.
Norwich launched plenty of promising attacks of their own, but they generally lacked any penetration and Andre Brooks' close-range effort into the side netting on 25 minutes was the closest they came to breaking the deadlock in the opening period.
Cardiff took a little over two minutes to get their noses in front after the break as Alex Robertson's inswinging free-kick to the back post was missed by home defence and Salech was on hand to stroke the ball into the bottom corner for his ninth goal of the season.
Norwich responded well and should have been back on level terms on the hour mark when Anthony Musuba bore down on goal from the left only to screw his shot horribly wide.
But the home faithful did not have to wait long for an equaliser. On 62 minutes the visitors unwisely left Maghoma with some space on the edge of the area and the in-form midfielder curled a delightful shot beyond the reach of Trott and into the far corner.
The momentum was now very much with the Canaries and they completed a swift turnaround by going ahead from the spot in the 68th minute. Ronan Kpakio was penalised for bring down Brooks as he made his way to the byline and although Trott saved Kvistgaarden's penalty, the Danish striker had no problem converting the rebound to make it 2-1.
Salech had a header rightly ruled out for offside as Cardiff sought a response while at the other end substitutes Lucien Mahovo and Jovon Makama were both inches away from stretching Norwich's lead.
Cardiff top scorer Jack Moylan was foiled by a good stop from Grimshaw late on as the home side notched up another win.

items.title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
items.summary:
Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small
items.text:
Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.
Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan, 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.
Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
Algorithms making life-and-death decisions
"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."
No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.
"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
A "nothing burger"
The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.
"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.
"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."
But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

items.title: Could Iran reverse its stated policy of a civil-only nuclear programme?
items.summary:
Could Iran reverse its stated policy of a civil-only nuclear programme?
Iran’s FM Araghchi says there is ‘major strategic debate’ about the future of Iran’s nuclear doctrine.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the country’s stockpile of enriched uranium will be used according to its nee
items.text:
Could Iran reverse its stated policy of a civil-only nuclear programme?
Iran’s FM Araghchi says there is ‘major strategic debate’ about the future of Iran’s nuclear doctrine.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the country’s stockpile of enriched uranium will be used according to its needs, “however they are defined”, as he spoke about possible changes to Iran’s longstanding nuclear doctrine.
Araghchi’s comments during an interview with Iranian media on Saturday have increased speculation that Iran may be moving away from its policy of limiting its nuclear programme to civilian purposes amid its conflict with the United States.
The future of Iran’s nuclear programme has become a major sticking point in efforts to end the war, with Washington insisting that it must have guarantees that Iran will never develop a nuclear weapon before it will agree to a full ceasefire.
So, is Iran’s nuclear policy changing, and what could that mean for the conflict?
What is Iran’s official nuclear policy?
Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes only, such as for electricity generation, medical research and agriculture.
This policy has been underlined by a decades-old religious decree, or fatwa, issued by the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, banning the development of nuclear weapons.
However, Iran has also insisted it has the right to enrich uranium for these purposes under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), which it joined in 1970. It has called this right “non-negotiable”.
What have Araghchi and other officials said?
In an interview with Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency on Saturday, Araghchi reiterated that Iran’s stockpile of enriched material would remain inside the country.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated in 2025 – before Israel launched strikes on Iran in June that year – that Iran had about 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched to about 60 percent. This is short of the 90 percent required for making nuclear weapons, but is the level at which it becomes much quicker to reach 90 percent. It is also far beyond the roughly 3 percent needed for power generation.
This material, Araghchi said during his interview, would “be used according to our needs however those needs are defined”.
Araghchi also made reference to an ongoing debate among lawmakers and officials in Iran about altering its nuclear doctrine, and said people on both sides of that debate have “strong arguments”.
“This is a major strategic debate, and there is nothing wrong with examining it seriously because it directly concerns national interests and security,” Araghchi said, adding that those in favour of reform argue Iran’s current approach of no nuclear weapons has “failed to protect” the country’s nuclear facilities, which have come under attack from US and Israeli forces both last year and this year.
However, Araghchi acknowledged that any official change to the policy would have “far-reaching consequences”.
“For now, our doctrine has not changed, and our official position remains the same,” he said.
Other Iranian officials have also spoken about a potential review of the country’s nuclear doctrine. Earlier this month, security chief Mohsen Rezaei said “there is a discussion on whether we want to continue to follow the previous nuclear doctrine in the event of a new war breaking out”, though he also stressed that Tehran has not yet made any change.
On November 12, Iran’s Assembly of Experts, the body that appoints the supreme leader, said reviewing “the country’s defence doctrine and establishing the necessary deterrence have become unavoidable necessities”.
Ali Fathollah-Nejad, a German-Iranian political scientist who directs the Center for Middle East and Global Order (CMEG), told Al Jazeera the move by the Assembly of Experts “appears to mark the first time a governing institution has endorsed this position”.
Why do the US and Israel think Iran is developing nuclear weapons?
Besides being a signatory to the NPT in 1970, Iran also initially complied with a nuclear agreement it struck with the US and other global powers in 2015 – the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), which required it to limit uranium enrichment to very low levels and undergo inspections.
But after Washington pulled out of the deal in 2018 under the first administration of US President Donald Trump, Tehran eventually went back to intensifying its nuclear programme and abandoned restrictions imposed by the deal.
In June 2025, the IAEA’s board of governors declared Iran was no longer complying with its commitment to international nuclear safeguards. Tehran rejected that report and accused the IAEA of giving a pretext for US and Israeli attacks targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, including Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, just days later during the 12-day war.
In March of this year, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said at least 200kg (440lbs) of Iran’s enriched material was believed to have survived the US-Israeli attacks and was likely buried underground in or near the Isfahan nuclear facility site.
Grossi has since said the agency cannot verify the amount or location of Iran’s enriched material due to a lack of access.
The IAEA has called Iran’s enrichment level “a matter of serious concern”, while the US has pointed to it as evidence that Iran is pursuing nuclear weapons despite its official policy.
“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel?” US Vice President JD Vance said in an interview with the Reuters news agency last month. “And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue.”
President Trump has repeatedly stated that Iran must never be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon.
Officials in Israel, which is widely believed to have its own undeclared nuclear weapons, have also long accused Iran of pursuing nuclear weapons.

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Southampton and Derby County at St Mary's on Saturday; Cyle Larin and Divin Mubama strike as Saints return to winning ways.
Saturday 21 November 2026 14:36, UK
Cyle Larin returned to action with a bang as Southampton extended their unbeaten run at home in the Championship to 18 games with a 2-0 victory over second-bottom Derby.
Larin turned in his eighth goal of the season but his first since 12 September - after a four-game drought and a hamstring problem.
Divin Mubama added a second in stoppage time as Saints shrugged off worries of failing against lower-placed sides - having dropped points against Watford, Preston, Wrexham, Lincoln and Bolton already this season.
Despite Tonda Eckert signing a new contract and Saints' incredible home form, St Mary's felt subdued on and off the pitch for much of the early kick-off.
The visitors, languishing in the relegation zone came in with a well-drilled defensive gameplan, and the hosts - without injured stars Leo Scienza, Caspar Jander and James Bree - struggled to break through.
Southampton's possession advantage did not translate to chances, as their only first-half shot on target saw Finn Azaz fashion a crafty flick at the near post.
They also struck the crossbar in a rare moment of quality, as Azaz dropped a ball into the six-yard box as Larin saw his stretched volley bounce back off the goal frame.
But it was the visitors that ended the half with more fluidity and had a trio of good efforts.
The lively Mohammed Fuseini flashed a snapshot across the face of goal. Carlton Morris looped a bouncing ball and forced Daniel Peretz into an acrobatic save, before Shane Duffy poked the resulting corner over.
The second half began in a similar manner with Saints struggling to unlock the defence, while the Rams' Fuseini tested Peretz at the other end.
Then, early in the second half, Southampton finally found some joy.
The ground was lifted when Azaz pirouetted in the box and lashed a shot at Jacob Widell Zetterstrom, before James Ward-Prowse's follow-up was blocked.
And that energy brought the opener, as Azaz, Ryan Manning and Samuel Edozie neatly played the ball around before Azaz's low cross was bundled in by Larin in the 57th minute.
The Canadian had missed the last four matches, and was a welcome return after attacking struggles at West Brom and Preston.
Azaz almost followed it up by getting on the scoresheet himself, but he scuffed straight at Zetterstrom from the edge of the area.
Ward-Prowse had a shot deflected over and had the ball in the net, pinging in from the half-way line when the whistle had already gone for an offside as the home team attempted to put the game to bed.
With Zetterstrom up for a corner in the fifth minute of added time, Man City loanee Mubama ran the length of the pitch on the counter to make it 2-0 - celebrating long before slotting home.

items.text:
Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word. They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android.
Chess.com’s next move is a new hub for classic games, from mahjong to sudoku
AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.
“Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with The Verge. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”
Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”
Classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.
The expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active users are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but said the site is “doing amazingly well.”
So, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.
AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 new games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI, mainly for coding tasks. He says they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.
“Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng says. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”
AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”
“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”
Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the company was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”
Elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI. Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more important. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.
Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng said it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

Millwall 0-1 Queens Park Rangers: Nicolas Madsen nets as QPR see off 10-man Lions
Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Millwall and Queens Park Rangers at the The Den on Saturday; Zak Sturge sees red early for Lions as Nicolas Madsen scores QPR winner.
Saturday 21 November 2026 14:34, UK
Nicolas Madsen's scruffy winner gave Queens Park Rangers their first away victory since August as they defeated Millwall 1-0 at The Den.
The result against their London rivals ensured the Hoops will end the weekend inside the play-off places in the Sky Bet Championship after they played the majority of the contest against 10 men following Zak Sturge's 15th-minute red card.
Despite a commendable defensive performance with depleted numbers, this was a third straight defeat for Millwall whose campaign continues to stutter.
Millwall began brightly, with their captain Jake Cooper nodding Camiel Neghli's cross into the path of Kyrell Lisbie - whose shot from an acute angle was saved by QPR goalkeeper Pierce Charles.
Ilias Chair tried to catch out Millwall's keeper, the returning Lukas Jensen, by trying his luck from just inside the Lions' half, with his audacious effort dipping wide.
Then came a big blow for the home side when Sturge was shown a straight red card for tripping Paul Smyth just outside the area as the last defender.
Smyth was then involved in an altercation on the touchline in the 24th minute that led to Millwall boss Alex Neil being shown a yellow card as the temperature in this London derby simmered.
Just when it looked as though the Lions would hold out until half-time, QPR took the lead in first-half stoppage time as Jensen first saved from Chair before Madsen's follow-up crossed the line despite Caleb Taylor's attempted heroics.
Millwall had goalkeeping coach Dean Thornton sent from the dugout in the aftermath and, short on numbers on the pitch, it looked a long way back for them in the second half.
The Hoops brought on Japanese midfielder Koki Saito at the break and he almost struck within six minutes of the restart when his shot from outside the box was pushed behind by Jensen.
Chair then curled a shot from the edge of the area narrowly wide and at this point it looked just a matter of time until the dominant visitors would score again.
But they were having a hard time of making all their possession count, with Richard Kone having a shot comfortably saved by Jensen as the match ticked towards the final 15 minutes.
QPR sub Karamoko Dembele had a good chance to make the game safe but his effort from Glen Kamara's cut-back went wide.
Jake Clarke-Salter was then narrowly off target from 25 yards in the 90th minute for the Hoops, for whom one goal proved to be enough.

items.text:
Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren't presented as evidence during the trial.
Juror says Rinderknecht's own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict
Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
"It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said. "After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he's guilty."
Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a "lack of information" presented to the jury about the technical review.
In the end, it was Rinderknecht's own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.
"Stating that he was up on the hill, didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night," Cameron said.
Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been 'mad at everything'
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.
Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.
After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.
Defense argues fire's origin is unproven
Haney cast doubt on the government's case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.
Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors' request to strike his testimony.
Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."
Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnes

items.title: Madrid chief Pérez: "outrageous" that LaLiga president Tebas hasn't resigned
items.summary: Florentino Pérez hit out at Javier Tebas -- saying it was "outrageous" that the LaLiga president had not resigned his post -- and slammed Spanish football's handling of the Negreira case in a speech to Real Madrid members on Saturday, while also signalling a closer working relationship with former a
items.text:
Florentino Pérez hit out at Javier Tebas -- saying it was "outrageous" that the LaLiga president had not resigned his post -- and slammed Spanish football's handling of the Negreira case in a speech to Real Madrid members on Saturday, while also signalling a closer working relationship with former adversaries UEFA.
Pérez, who was re-elected as Madrid president earlier this year, delivered a 45-minute speech at the club's annual assembly, which began with applause for former tennis star Rafael Nadal, as he joined Madrid's board of directors.
In recent years, Pérez has used the assembly to deliver updates on a series of conflicts involving Madrid and football's governing bodies, including the attempted breakaway European Superleague, as well as the failure to bring the Negreira investigation -- into Barcelona's decades-long payments to Spain's former vice-president of refereeing -- to a conclusion.
"The Negreira case isn't just a problem for Real Madrid," Pérez said. "What happened was extraordinarily serious... It's not for me to judge anyone. The courts and UEFA will do that. But as Real Madrid president, I won't stop until those responsible are held accountable.
"It seems like the whole system wants us to forget about what happened, and talk about something else. The head of referees said we should move on. How are we going to move on? The worst is Tebas, who instead of helping to clarify it all, has chosen to attack Real Madrid every day... It's outrageous that he hasn't resigned."
Last month, Madrid called for Tebas to quit after he compared the club's communications policy to Nazi minister Joseph Goebbels, saying Madrid's use of its club TV channel "recalls propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels."
Tebas responded to Pérez's speech in a series of posts on X on Saturday.
"Florentino, before you ask for my resignation again, read my Oct. 16 post in full," he said. "There I explained which Real Madrid TV communication techniques I was criticizing, and why. I stand by what I wrote. I have committed no wrongdoing."
Pérez also discussed Madrid's changing relationship with UEFA and European Football Clubs (formerly the European Club Association) in the wake of the Superleague row, following an agreement reached between the three parties in February.
"We've had important differences, but we've always put football's interests first," Pérez said, before appearing to break news of a joint initiative which would meet one of the Superleague's stated goals: broadcasting games free-to-air.
"From next season, the best European games will be shown for free in India on a new platform. It's a way of testing this model, in one of the biggest countries in the world... It's the same process that FIFA followed with the Club World Cup. I also announce that Real Madrid are working to return to the EFC, and to UEFA's committees. We'll push for all these initiatives from the inside."
"Now it turns out that Florentino is the spokesperson for UEFA, the EFC and [their joint venture] UC3," Tebas responded. "He announces their TV plans before they do themselves."
- Tennis great Rafa Nadal accepts Real Madrid offer to join board of directors
- Veteran GK Courtois extends Real Madrid contract to 2028
- José Mourinho wants Vinícius Jr. to move on from summer woes
Pérez failed to elaborate on a plan which was much debated during Madrid's presidential elections earlier this year, to change the club's ownership structure by selling a percentage to an external investor.
Madrid are one of just four Spanish football clubs which are owned by their members. "I want to say again that Real Madrid won't be sold, it will never be sold," Pérez said on Saturday. "It belongs to its members... A year ago, I told you that we had to protect ourselves from threats both outside and inside. This year we've seen that, during the electoral campaign.
"I want you to leave here with a clear idea. Real Madrid is ours, not just in a romantic way, but truly. We need the members, more than ever, to be the active guardians of our financial wealth. That's why we're working on this reform, to protect the heritage that we've built. We won't adopt any decision that risks the ownership of the club by its members."
Later, facing questions from club members, Pérez called on fans not to whistle the players at the Bernabéu when the team underperforms.
"I just want to say one thing: you can't whistle our players," Pérez said. "The enemy is on the outside, not at home... I'd ask you never to support those whistles, which are influenced by some of the media."
The club's CEO, José Ángel Sánchez, also claimed there was now "no legal impediment" to holding concerts at the Bernabéu, after they were halted following noise concerns from neighbours.
"The acoustic work has finished, and it's improved a lot," Sánchez said. "We're thinking about bringing the concerts back soon."

items.text:
Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
- Published
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

Nikhil Chaudhary blasted 66 and a late cameo from Jack Edwards helped Australia edge past England by
items.text:
Chaudhary helps Australia beat England in T20 shake-off of scandal-hit run
Australia beat England by three wickets with only one ball to spare as Nikhil Chaudhary’s 66 leads the charge in Melbourne.
Nikhil Chaudhary blasted 66 and a late cameo from Jack Edwards helped Australia edge past England by three wickets with a ball to spare in the opening T20 International of the series.
Chaudhary’s 38-ball knock was crucial, but it was Edwards’ late flurry that got the job done, with the fast-bowler hitting an unbeaten 25 off 11 as they chased down a victory target of 188 on Saturday.
It ensured they took a 1-0 lead in the five-match series and temporarily lifted some of the clouds hanging over Australian cricket. Four of the country’s previous five matches have resulted in defeats, including a 2-1 One-Day International home series defeat by England.
The win also came on the day that Cricket Australia backed Pat Cummins to stay on as Test captain, despite continued allegations that he and the rest of the 2018 team were aware of the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball during their tour of South Africa.
England captain Harry Brook’s quickfire 65 had guided the visitors to 187-9 – the highest T20I score at the Melbourne Cricket Ground – but Australia’s response had already begun prior to the chase when their bowlers restricted the end of the tourists’ innings that had looked set to comfortably pass 200.
“Right, there is the future of the Australian cricket side with those young guys in it,” said Australia captain Mitchell Marsh.
“They’re a great bunch. Hopefully a win like that gives them a lot of confidence that they all belong.”
The run chase started badly for Australia with opener Jake Fraser-McGurk falling to just his third ball, undone by the spin of Liam Dawson.
Australia got going when debutant Sam Harper came in and took 20 off Jamie Overton’s first over.
But the 29-year-old swung the bat once too often and departed for 32 off 15 balls, earning new England fast-bowler Henry Crocombe a first T20 wicket.
They were 86-2 at the halfway mark, and when Dawson took a stunning catch to remove Marsh for 37, Australia’s hopes appeared to rest with Tim David.
But the big-hitter struggled to get going and was out for 20, leaving Chaudhary, in only his fourth T20 for Australia, in charge.
He departed chasing another boundary, only for Edwards to step up.
They needed 11 of the last over from Sam Curran, and when Edwards smacked a six off the first delivery, they were on their way to the win.
“Very entertaining to go down to the last couple of balls,” said Brook. “We were probably 10 runs short of what we needed on that surface.”
Earlier, England lost opener Phil Salt to the first ball and they were 13-2 in the third over after Aneurin Donald was also removed cheaply for 10.
But Brook went to town, smacking three straight sixes from paceman Riley Meredith.
He reached 50 off 20 deliveries before his fiery knock ended when he got a faint outside edge off Chaudhary to wicketkeeper Harper.
Tom Banton was put down on 11, among six dropped catches by Australia, but his luck ran out on 39 when another debutant, Lachlan Shaw, held on to a difficult chance.
The wickets kept tumbling with Curran caught out on 21 and Will Jacks out lbw for three, with Jordan Cox hitting 27 to keep the scoreboard moving.

Perspective: Defining 'human'
The Cambridge Dictionary has revealed its Word of the Year for 2026. It won't need much explanation. Unlike "parasocial," their 2025 word, which refers to an unreciprocated emotional connection, perhaps with a chatbot, or 2018's word, "nomophobia," which is an irrationa
items.text:
Perspective: Defining 'human'
The Cambridge Dictionary has revealed its Word of the Year for 2026. It won't need much explanation. Unlike "parasocial," their 2025 word, which refers to an unreciprocated emotional connection, perhaps with a chatbot, or 2018's word, "nomophobia," which is an irrational fear of having no mobile phone service–although, given all the recent cyber-struggles, why would that be irrational?
The Cambridge 2026 World of the Year is … human. As in us. And perhaps humanity could stand some recognition in times when people see Artificial Intelligence seep into our lives the way ancient dinosaurs may have watched the asteroid plunge through the atmosphere, and think, "They're coming for us!" though I suspect a few T-Rexes might have said, "Hey, don't worry! We're too big to fail!"
Cambridge defines "human" as: "(h)aving the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines," but they don't specify much about what those qualities, faults and feelings are.
I'd say that humans have a sense of responsibility. We can say, "I'm sorry, that's my fault," when we screw up or fall short, as opposed to screens that just flash, SYSTEM OVERLOAD or UPDATE IN PROGRESS, 12% COMPLETE.
Humans seek joy, not just continued existence. Laughter, tears, love, spice, poetry, and all that jazz, not just code or text. Humans like jokes and prayers. We're driven by feelings, not just steered by algorithms. Love, fear, anger, desire, joy, and courage, excited by events, nerves and hormones – combine to make us unpredictable, irreverent and unreliable. But our experiences can also instill judgement; an appreciation for what's important; what endures; and what makes the lives we have worth living and savoring.
Making human the 2026 Word of the Year may remind us that we human beings, unlike any robots we have yet devised, have a sense of our own fragility. We know we don't last forever. And so it is important to strive, laugh, and love while we have the chance. The Cambridge dictionary leaves what human truly means to us.

items.summary:
Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in
items.text:
Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

items.text:
Riemann hypothesis: Has the world’s most famous maths problem been cracked?
Mathematicians say the claimed proof, made with Claude, could be historic, but it may take weeks to understand it.
A mathematician from the tech giant Anthropic claims to have proven one of the world’s most famous – and most elusive – maths problems with the help of AI.
Levent Alpoge wrote on his website on Friday: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”
If his claim holds up, the proof he says he has would settle a question that has defeated mathematicians for 167 years. Independent experts are now trying to verify it, but so far no human has read through the entire argument.
Here is what we know.
What is the Riemann hypothesis?
First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics.
Prime numbers are whole numbers which can be divided only by one and themselves, such as 2, 3, 5 and 7. They appear to be scattered along the number line with no obvious pattern but the Riemann hypothesis proposes that their overall distribution actually follows a deep, hidden order – just one that humans have yet to identify.
“The Riemann hypothesis is the most famous and important unsolved problem in mathematics,” Abhishek Saha, professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.
“The patterns of the primes are encoded in a mathematical object called the Riemann zeta function, introduced by Bernhard Riemann in 1859.”
It is one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1m award.
What has the Anthropic mathematician claimed?
Alpoge, a member of the company’s technical staff, made the announcement on Friday in a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said the proof he has found covers the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which extends the original conjecture to a broader family of mathematical functions.
He did not publish a conventional paper. Alpoge released the argument in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks reasoning step by step. He was open about how much of the work was Claude’s, writing that “Claude far outpaced me near the finish line”.
Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said nobody yet understands what the proof actually shows.
“At the minute, we don’t even know why the theorem is true,” he told Al Jazeera. “It’s 17 million lines of Lean code, and this might correspond to tens of thousands of pages of mathematics. We don’t even yet know how much of this mathematics is new ideas, how much of it is just sort of standard stuff the machine just had to develop.
“At the minute, the proof is just millions of lines of gobbledygook written in a strange programming language,” he said. “And right now, as we speak, there’s people all over the world who are translating parts of this programming language back into English.”
He expects answers to come fairly soon, however. “Experience shows you that you give the humans the Lean code, and within a week or two, they have a much better understanding of what’s actually going on in this code,” he said.
Why is the Riemann hypothesis so important?
“The implications of this hypothesis extend across large parts of mathematics, and hundreds of other mathematical results have been proved assuming this hypothesis is true,” Saha said. “A proof would settle a question that has occupied some of the greatest mathematical minds for over 160 years.”
Buzzard said the result also matters beyond pure mathematics, including for internet security.
“We know there are some algorithms that we run where they’re very quick, but we don’t actually know for sure if they work,” he said. “They seem to work, and we know that if the generalised Riemann hypothesis is true, then they do work.”
He said cryptographers had long worked on the assumption that the Riemann hypothesis is true. “In practice, people do tend to assume that the Riemann hypothesis is true because it’s a viable hypothesis to assume, because there’s so much evidence that it’s true,” he said. “But we can sleep slightly safer in our beds at night because it is true.”
Buzzard said the result stands out among recent AI breakthroughs in mathematics. He compared it with the Navier-Stokes problem, another Millennium Prize problem, which OpenAI said an unreleased AI model had solved in September. “That one doesn’t really have any applications at all,” he said, calling it “just of theoretical interest”. “Whereas the Riemann hypothesis has applications to neighbouring fields.
“It’s a very hard problem, but it’s definitely not the hardest problem in mathematics,” he said, pointing to even stronger versions such as the “extended Riemann hypothesis and the grand Riemann hypothesis”.
“The Riemann hypothesis is just, in some sense, at the foot of a mountain,” he said. “We’re beginning our trek up the mountain with this theorem.”
Why has it remained so elusive for so long?
“The problem is relatively simple to state, but extraordinarily difficult to prove,” Saha said. “Mathematicians have developed vast amounts of sophisticated theory in their attempts to solve it, but none of the techniques developed over the past 167 years has been sufficient. The direct methods have all been tried, and none of them come close to resolving it.
“Until very recently, most mathematicians, myself included, believed that a proof would require substantial new mathematical theories, perhaps developed over the next few decades.”
He said the claimed proof had overturned his expectations. “My own intuition was that we were still several years away from a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. This claimed proof, if correct, shatters my model of reality,” he said.

items.text:
Russia says Kaliningrad-bound ship struck by drones in Gulf of Finland
Two drones attack a cargo ship close to Russia’s maritime border, causing damage and crew evacuation.
Two drones have struck a cargo ship bound for Russia’s exclave Kaliningrad in international waters of the Gulf of Finland, close to Russia’s maritime border, according to a senior Russian official.
The attack happened west of Gogland Island on Saturday morning, with Finland instating air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.
It is not clear who was behind the attack.
Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, said the vessel’s crew were being evacuated and the damage had yet to be fully assessed.
“Three nautical miles from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max.
Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.
The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members. It connects Russia’s former capital of St Petersburg with its Kaliningrad enclave by sea.
Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with the vessel sustaining damage, and dispatched Finnish Border Guard units to the scene.
The ministry said air and sea traffic restrictions were a precaution in case further drones needed to be intercepted, adding that Finland had notified its allies of the incident.
“A Russian cargo ship is on fire in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Finnish Border Guard is leading the maritime rescue operation and is preparing for potential environmental damage control within Finland’s area of responsibility,” Finland’s Border Guard said on its official website.
Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.
Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki said it had raised concerns about striking in the area with Kyiv afterwards.
Saturday’s attack has not been attributed to anyone.
